transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

I guess what brings me in is… it’s this reaction I’m having at work, mostly around the stockroom. If I even think there might be a bat in there, or something flapping around, my body just reacts right away. Like, before I can even talk myself through it, my heart kind of jumps, I start sweating, and I get this really strong feeling that I need to get out of there immediately.

It’s not just “oh, that’s unpleasant” — it feels like my whole body is telling me to leave right then. And I know it probably sounds kind of specific, but it’s been bothering me enough that I figured I should talk to someone about it.
Is it specifically bats that trigger this reaction, or would other animals or situations cause a similar response?

It’s mostly bats, yeah. Or… I guess anything that my brain reads as a bat for even half a second. Like if I’m in the back hallway and something flutters quickly, or I catch a dark shape out of the corner of my eye, my mind just jumps straight to “bat,” and then it’s like I’m in danger right then.

The frustrating thing is I do know, logically, that a bat in the store probably isn’t going to hurt me. I can say that sitting here. But in the moment, it doesn’t feel like that matters. If it looks like one, or sounds like one, or even moves in that quick flapping way, my body and my head react like it’s an actual threat.
Does this reaction to bats or things that resemble bats happen only at work, or have you experienced it in other places as well?

I’m not totally sure how to answer that, because I mostly notice it at work, since that’s where I’m around the stockroom and the back areas more. That’s the place my mind goes to right away when I think about it.

I mean, I don’t have a lot of examples outside of work that are as clear. It’s not like I’m walking around all day everywhere expecting bats, if that makes sense. But I also don’t know if that’s because it really only happens at work, or because I’m not usually in places where I’d think there could be one. Like at home I’m not usually dealing with dark storage rooms or back hallways, so it just doesn’t come up in the same way.

So… I guess the honest answer is, I’ve mainly experienced it at work, and I haven’t really noticed it much in other places.
How long have you been experiencing this reaction to bats or things that resemble bats?

It’s been about two years now, I think. It started after this one night at work when I was on a receiving shift, and a bat somehow got into the back corridor.

Before that, I mean, I don’t remember reacting this strongly. I probably wouldn’t have liked seeing one, but it wasn’t like this. That night kind of sticks in my head, because it was back in that corridor area and it was moving around, and ever since then, anything that reminds me of that has set me off. So… yeah, roughly two years.
Do you find yourself feeling anxious or on edge in situations that have nothing to do with bats?

Um… I don’t think so? Not in the same way, at least. I mean, everybody gets stressed, right—work can be annoying, money stuff, customers being difficult, normal life things—but I don’t walk around generally feeling on edge for no reason, if that’s what you mean.

The anxious feeling I’m talking about is pretty tied to the bat thing, or places where I start thinking there could be one. If I’m just at home watching TV or doing errands or something, I’m not usually tense like that. At least I haven’t really noticed it.

I guess sometimes after something reminds me of it, I might stay a little keyed up for a while, but I wouldn’t say I’m anxious all the time or in situations that have nothing to do with bats. It’s more like my brain needs some kind of trigger to go there.
Do you find yourself avoiding certain places or activities because you're afraid of encountering a bat?

Yeah… I do. More than I probably want to admit, honestly.

At work especially, I’ve been swapping out closing shifts when I can, because closing is when I end up around the back areas more, and it’s darker and quieter and my mind starts going there. I don’t always say exactly why, either — I’ll just try to trade with somebody or make it sound like a scheduling thing, because it feels embarrassing to say, “I don’t want to be back there because I’m scared there might be a bat.”

And if I have to go near the loading area, I’ll take the long way around instead of going the normal way, even if it’s kind of ridiculous and takes extra time. I know that sounds like a small thing, but I’ll actually plan my route through the store around avoiding that part if I can.

Then there are times I can’t avoid it, like if I have to check the stairwell or something. I’ll still do it, but I make myself do it really fast. I’ll have my phone in my hand, like having the flashlight ready or just… I don’t know, like it makes me feel less trapped. But I’m scared the whole time, and I’m basically trying to get in and out as quickly as possible.
Has avoiding places where you might encounter bats started to affect your personal life or relationships outside of work?

Yeah… I mean, outside of work, maybe not so much with friends or dating or anything like that, but it’s definitely affecting my life in a bigger way because of work. Work is kind of where everything is tied together for me right now.

My manager has started noticing that I keep trying to trade out of closing duties, and I think at first he maybe thought it was just normal schedule stuff, but now it’s happened enough that he’s questioning it. And the closing shift is a big deal because if you’re going to be a shift lead, you have to be someone they can count on after hours — like doing the checks, making sure the back areas are handled, that sort of thing.

And that’s the part that really bothers me, because I’ve been trying to work toward a more permanent management position. It’s not like I’m just avoiding some little inconvenience. This could actually cost me that opportunity if they decide I’m not dependable enough.

My manager hasn’t flat-out said, “You’re not getting it,” but I can tell he’s wondering if I can handle it. He’s asked why I’m always switching those shifts, and I don’t really know how to explain it without sounding ridiculous. So I give these vague answers, which probably makes me look worse.

So, yeah… it’s not just embarrassing anymore. It feels like this thing could mess up something I’ve been working toward.
Are there any situations outside of work where you feel like your fear of bats is holding you back or causing you significant distress?

Outside of work… I’m trying to think. Not really in a big way, I don’t think. I mean, I don’t love being outside at night if something makes me think about bats, like if it’s really dark or there are trees overhead or something, but I can’t say I’ve stopped seeing people or stopped doing normal life stuff because of it.

Most of the real problem is tied to work, because that’s where I feel like I might actually have to go into those back areas or deal with it if one showed up. Outside work, I can usually just… not put myself in that situation, I guess, or it doesn’t come up as much.

So I wouldn’t say it’s causing major problems in my personal life, at least not that I’ve noticed. It’s more like an uncomfortable thought here and there, unless something specifically reminds me of it.
Are you avoiding any social activities or hobbies outside of work because of your fear of bats?

Not really social activities or hobbies, no… at least I don’t think so. I mean, I’m not skipping parties or avoiding friends because of bats or anything like that.

It’s more that the avoiding shows up at work. Like I said, I’ve been swapping out closing shifts when I can, because those are the times I feel like I’m more likely to have to go through the darker back areas. And I’ll take the long way around the loading area instead of just walking through it normally, even if it makes no sense time-wise. If I have to check the stairwell, I’ll do it, but I kind of rush through it with my phone in my hand, like I’m ready to turn the flashlight on or call someone, and I’m scared the whole time.

So outside of work, no, not in a major way. But at work it’s definitely making me avoid things or get through them as fast as possible.
Are you finding that your fear of bats is affecting your ability to enjoy or participate in daily activities outside of your job?

I don’t think so, not in any clear way. Like, day-to-day outside of work, I’m still doing the normal things I need to do. I go to the store, I see people, I can go out to eat or whatever. I’m not sitting at home refusing to leave because of it.

I mean, if I’m outside at night and something makes me think about bats — like if it’s quiet and dark, or I’m walking near trees — then I might feel uncomfortable, and I’ll probably look around more than I need to. But I wouldn’t say it’s stopping me from enjoying my life outside of work in a major way.

It’s really more that work puts me in situations where I feel like I can’t just avoid it without consequences. Outside of work, it’s more like… if I don’t want to walk through some dark area, I just don’t, and nobody really notices or cares. So I haven’t noticed it affecting my daily activities outside my job too much.
Are you ever worried that your fear of bats might spread to other things or situations, making it harder for you to manage your daily life?

I don’t know that I’ve thought about it that way, honestly. Like… “spread” to other things? I guess I worry sometimes that if I keep avoiding the bat-related stuff at work, maybe I’ll get more and more nervous about those areas in general, even if there isn’t actually a bat there. But I’m not sure if that’s what you mean.

I haven’t really noticed it turning into a fear of, like, all animals or being outside in general or anything like that. It still feels pretty specifically tied to bats, or places where I imagine one could be hiding. Like dark corners, stairwells, the loading area—those kinds of spots. But I don’t know if I’m afraid of the place itself, or if my brain is just going, “That’s where a bat could be.”

So… I guess I’m a little worried it could get harder to manage if I let it keep controlling what I do, but I can’t say it has spread in a big way so far. At least not that I’ve clearly noticed.
Has your fear of bats affected your relationships with family or friends in any way?

Not that I’ve really noticed, no. I mean, my family and friends know I don’t like bats, or at least I think they’ve picked up on it, but it hasn’t turned into arguments or anything like that.

I’m not avoiding seeing them because of it, and I’m not asking people to change plans around me, at least not in any big way. If someone wanted to do something outdoors at night, I might feel a little tense depending on where it was, but I don’t think it’s gotten to the point where it’s affecting the relationship itself.

At work it feels more obvious because there are certain areas I have to deal with, but with family or friends, I guess it just doesn’t come up that much. So… no, I wouldn’t say it’s really affected my relationships.
Are there any parts of your daily routine that you've had to change because of your fear of bats?

Yeah… I mean, not my whole daily routine, but there are definitely parts of it I’ve adjusted, mostly around work.

The biggest thing is closing shifts. I’ve been trying to swap out of those when I can, or trade with somebody else, because that’s when I get more nervous about running into bats, especially around the back areas or when it’s darker. I don’t always say the full reason, honestly. Sometimes I’ll just say I have something going on or ask if someone wants to switch, but in my head it’s really because I don’t want to be there at that time.

And then at work I’ll take the long way around the loading area instead of going through it directly. It’s kind of embarrassing because it adds time and it probably looks unnecessary, but I just feel better not going through that spot if I can avoid it. If I have to pass by it, I’m kind of tense the whole time.

The stairwell is another one. If I have to check it, I’ll still do it, but I do it really fast. I’ll hold my phone in my hand, like that somehow makes me feel more prepared, and I’ll kind of shine the light or keep it ready. I know it probably looks ridiculous, but I’m scared the whole time, and I’m just trying to get in and out as quickly as possible.

So, yeah, I guess I have changed some things. It’s not like every minute of my day is different, but I’m definitely planning around it more than I’d like to admit.
Are you finding that your fear of bats is significantly impacting your overall quality of life?

Yeah… I think it is, more than I wanted to admit at first. I was kind of telling myself it was just an inconvenience, like, “Okay, I don’t like bats, so I avoid a couple areas at work,” but it’s starting to affect something bigger.

My manager has noticed that I keep trying to trade out of closing duties, and that I’m not as dependable when it comes to those after-hours checks. And I get why that looks bad from their side, because if you’re supposed to be a shift lead, you can’t just be unavailable for certain parts of the job. But for me, those are the exact parts that make me feel like I can’t handle it.

The hard part is I’ve been working toward a permanent management position, and now I feel like this could actually cost me that. My manager has started questioning whether I can handle the shift lead role, and that really bothers me because I don’t want to be seen as unreliable. I’ve worked hard to get to that point.

So, yeah, I’d say it’s impacting my quality of life because it’s not just me being uncomfortable anymore. It’s affecting my job and where I might be headed with it, and that’s pretty stressful.
Are you finding that your fear of bats is causing you to avoid social interactions or events with friends or family?

No, I don’t think so. Not really with friends or family.

Like, if someone invites me to dinner or to come over, I’m not avoiding that because of bats. I still see people, I still talk to them, I still go to normal stuff. It’s not like I’m isolating myself or canceling plans all the time because of it.

I guess if there was something very specific, like someone wanted to go walking around outside at night in a wooded area or something, I might feel uneasy and maybe try to steer it toward something else. But that honestly doesn’t come up much in my social life. Most of the problem is more tied to work situations, not family gatherings or hanging out with friends.

So, no… I wouldn’t say it’s causing me to avoid social interactions or events with them.
Have you started to fear other animals or creatures besides bats?

No… I don’t think it’s really spread to other animals, if that’s what you mean. Like, I’m not suddenly scared of dogs or birds or bugs in general.

It’s more that if something reminds me of a bat, that’s when I react. Like if I see a quick flutter in the back hallway at work, or something dark moves fast out of the corner of my eye, my brain just jumps straight to “bat” before I even know what I’m looking at. And I know, logically, a bat in the store probably isn’t going to hurt me. I can say that sitting here. But in the moment, it doesn’t feel harmless. My body reacts like I’m in actual danger.

So I wouldn’t say I’m afraid of other creatures exactly. It’s more anything that looks like it could be one, or moves like one, sets me off.
Are there any other areas of your life, beyond work, where you feel like your fear of bats is causing you significant distress or problems?

I’m not sure there’s a big area outside of work where it’s causing major problems, honestly. I mean, I think about it sometimes, especially if I’m somewhere at night or near places where I imagine bats could be, but it’s not like it’s taking over my whole life outside the job.

Most of the actual distress is tied to those work situations, because that’s where I feel like I might run into one and also where I feel pressured to still do what I’m supposed to do. Outside of that, I can usually just avoid thinking about it or not put myself in those situations.

So… no, I wouldn’t say there’s another major area beyond work where it’s really causing significant problems. At least not that I’ve noticed.
Are there any daily activities outside of work that you used to enjoy but no longer do because of your fear of bats?

No, I don’t think so. I can’t really point to a daily activity outside of work that I used to enjoy and then stopped doing because of bats.

I mean, I’m trying to think through my normal routine — errands, going to the store, seeing people, being at home, that kind of thing — and I don’t feel like there’s something obvious where I’d say, “I don’t do that anymore because I’m afraid of bats.” It’s not like I stopped going out during the day or stopped doing hobbies or anything like that.

Maybe if something involved being outside at night, I might be more aware of it or feel uncomfortable, but I wouldn’t say there’s a regular activity I’ve given up. Most of it is more that I get anxious in certain situations where I think one could show up, but outside of work it hasn’t really changed my day-to-day life in a big way.
Have you started to fear other things that are not bats but might remind you of them, such as other flying creatures or dark places?

Yeah… kind of, but not exactly in the sense that I’m afraid of, like, all flying things now. I wouldn’t say I’m scared of birds or moths as a category. It’s more the resemblance, or the sudden movement.

Like if I’m in the back hallway at work and I see something dark move fast, or there’s a quick flutter near the ceiling or in the corner of my eye, my mind doesn’t stop and calmly figure out what it is. It just jumps straight to “bat.” And then my body reacts before I’ve even really seen anything clearly.

I know, sitting here, that even if there was a bat in the store it probably isn’t going to hurt me. I can say that and understand it. But in the moment, when something looks like one or moves like one, it feels like I’m in actual danger. Like I need to get away or brace myself or something.

So dark places by themselves… I don’t know if I’d say I’m afraid of darkness generally. But a dark hallway or a shadowy area where I could imagine something fluttering around, that can set me on edge because it makes me think there might be one there.

It’s really more that work puts me in situations where I feel like I can’t just avoid it without consequences. Outside of work, it’s more like… if I don’t want to walk through some dark area, I just don’t, and nobody really notices or cares. So I haven’t noticed it affecting my daily activities outside my job too much.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's fear of bats is interfering with their daily life to the extent that it could indicate a more generalized anxiety disorder
doctor.question: Are you ever worried that your fear of bats might spread to other things or situations, making it harder for you to manage your daily life?

patient.answer:

But I’m not sure if that’s what you mean.

I haven’t really noticed it turning into a fear of, like, all animals or being outside in general or anything like that. It still feels pretty specifically tied to bats, or places where I imagine one could be hiding. Like dark corners, stairwells, the loading area—those kinds of spots. But I don’t know if I’m afraid of the place itself, or if my brain is just going, “That’s where a bat could be.”

So… I guess I’m a little worried it could get harder to manage if I let it keep controlling what I do, but I can’t say it has spread in a big way so far. At least not that I’ve clearly noticed.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's fear is interfering with their relationships
doctor.question: Has your fear of bats affected your relationships with family or friends in any way?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking specifically about effects on relationships with family or friends, but the symptom profile only covers phobic fear, immediate anxiety response, avoidance/endurance, work-related functional impairment, and duration; it does not include relationship impairment.

patient.answer:
Not that I’ve really noticed, no. I mean, my family and friends know I don’t like bats, or at least I think they’ve picked up on it, but it hasn’t turned into arguments or anything like that.

If someone wanted to do something outdoors at night, I might feel a little tense depending on where it was, but I don’t think it’s gotten to the point where it’s affecting the relationship itself.

At work it feels more obvious because there are certain areas I have to deal with, but with family or friends, I guess it just doesn’t come up that much. So… no, I wouldn’t say it’s really affected my relationships.

doctor.intent: determine if the fear is interfering with the patient's daily life in a significant way
doctor.question: Are there any parts of your daily routine that you've had to change because of your fear of bats?

target_item.name: Phobic_Avoidance_Endure
target_item.manifestation: I've been swapping out closing shifts, taking the long way around the loading area, and when I have to check the stairwell I make myself do it fast while holding my phone and feeling scared the whole time.
target_item.reason: The question asks about changes to daily routine because of the fear, which directly relates to avoiding bat-related situations or enduring them with distress.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I mean, not my whole daily routine, but there are definitely parts of it I’ve adjusted, mostly around work.

The biggest thing is closing shifts. I’ve been trying to swap out of those when I can, or trade with somebody else, because that’s when I get more nervous about running into bats, especially around the back areas or when it’s darker. I don’t always say the full reason, honestly. Sometimes I’ll just say I have something going on or ask if someone wants to switch, but in my head it’s really because I don’t want to be there at that time.

And then at work I’ll take the long way around the loading area instead of going through it directly. It’s kind of embarrassing because it adds time and it probably looks unnecessary, but I just feel better not going through that spot if I can avoid it. If I have to pass by it, I’m kind of tense the whole time.

The stairwell is another one. If I have to check it, I’ll still do it, but I do it really fast. I’ll hold my phone in my hand, like that somehow makes me feel more prepared, and I’ll kind of shine the light or keep it ready. I know it probably looks ridiculous, but I’m scared the whole time, and I’m just trying to get in and out as quickly as possible.

So, yeah, I guess I have changed some things. It’s not like every minute of my day is different, but I’m definitely planning around it more than I’d like to admit.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's fear is interfering with their daily life outside of work to a significant degree
doctor.question: Are you finding that your fear of bats is significantly impacting your overall quality of life?

My manager has noticed that I keep trying to trade out of closing duties, and that I’m not as dependable when it comes to those after-hours checks. And I get why that looks bad from their side, because if you’re supposed to be a shift lead, you can’t just be unavailable for certain parts of the job. But for me, those are the exact parts that make me feel like I can’t handle it.

The hard part is I’ve been working toward a permanent management position, and now I feel like this could actually cost me that. My manager has started questioning whether I can handle the shift lead role, and that really bothers me because I don’t want to be seen as unreliable. I’ve worked hard to get to that point.

So, yeah, I’d say it’s impacting my quality of life because it’s not just me being uncomfortable anymore. It’s affecting my job and where I might be headed with it, and that’s pretty stressful.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's fear is generalized to other animals
doctor.question: Have you started to fear other animals or creatures besides bats?

target_item.name: Specific_Phobic_Fear
target_item.manifestation: I know a bat in the store probably isn't going to hurt me, but if I see anything that looks like one or even a quick flutter in the back hallway, my mind treats it like I'm in real danger.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about the scope of the specific phobic fear—whether it is limited to bats or has generalized to other animals or creatures.

patient.answer:
No… I don’t think it’s really spread to other animals, if that’s what you mean. Like, I’m not suddenly scared of dogs or birds or bugs in general.

It’s more that if something reminds me of a bat, that’s when I react. Like if I see a quick flutter in the back hallway at work, or something dark moves fast out of the corner of my eye, my brain just jumps straight to “bat” before I even know what I’m looking at. And I know, logically, a bat in the store probably isn’t going to hurt me. I can say that sitting here. But in the moment, it doesn’t feel harmless. My body reacts like I’m in actual danger.

So I wouldn’t say I’m afraid of other creatures exactly. It’s more anything that looks like it could be one, or moves like one, sets me off.

Most of the actual distress is tied to those work situations, because that’s where I feel like I might run into one and also where I feel pressured to still do what I’m supposed to do. Outside of that, I can usually just avoid thinking about it or not put myself in those situations.

So… no, I wouldn’t say there’s another major area beyond work where it’s really causing significant problems. At least not that I’ve noticed.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's fear is specific to bats or has generalized to other similar stimuli
doctor.question: Have you started to fear other things that are not bats but might remind you of them, such as other flying creatures or dark places?

patient.answer:
Yeah… kind of, but not exactly in the sense that I’m afraid of, like, all flying things now. I wouldn’t say I’m scared of birds or moths as a category. It’s more the resemblance, or the sudden movement.
